title: Errors, Debugging, and Testing
intro: Reliable software comes from reading failures clearly and preventing repeats. In this topic you will learn how Python exceptions communicate failure, how to handle expected errors without hiding bugs, and how tests lock in behavior so refactors stay safe. The focus is practical debugging discipline, not fear-driven trial and error.
mental_model: Exceptions are signals that normal flow broke. Tracebacks show where and why. Error handling should recover from expected failures and surface unexpected ones. Tests convert assumptions into repeatable checks. Debugging is a loop: reproduce, inspect, hypothesize, change one thing, verify.
must_know: Read traceback bottom-up: exception type/message, then your line, then call path.
Catch specific exceptions rather than using bare `except:`.
Raise clear exceptions when input violates function contracts.
Use finally or context managers for cleanup paths.
Test both normal and edge cases so debugging starts from stable expectations.
common_traps: Swallowing unexpected exceptions and losing debugging signals.
Changing multiple things at once while debugging.
Writing assertions without meaningful error intent.
Confusing temporary print-debugging with lasting test coverage.
interview: Explain why bare `except` is risky in production systems.
Walk through a traceback and identify first actionable line.
Design tests for boundary, invalid, and empty input cases.
Explain when to raise versus return sentinel values like None.
real_world: Automation scripts should surface actionable errors for missing config, malformed data, and command failures, not silently continue.
Backend teams rely on tests to prevent regressions when parser logic or validation rules evolve.
outcome: By the end of this topic, you should be able to read tracebacks, handle expected exceptions safely, raise clear errors for invalid states, and write focused tests that protect critical behavior.

lesson_sections.title: 1. Reading Tracebacks Effectively
lesson_sections.body: Tracebacks list call frames leading to failure. Start at the exception type and message, then locate the first line in your own code. This habit helps you avoid random changes and move directly to root-cause analysis.

lesson_sections.title: 2. Handling Expected Exceptions
lesson_sections.body: Use try/except for failures you expect and can recover from. Catch specific exception classes, not everything. This keeps normal failure paths safe while preserving visibility for unexpected bugs.

lesson_sections.title: 3. Raising Exceptions with Clear Messages
lesson_sections.body: When input or state violates a function contract, raise an appropriate exception with a useful message. Good error messages shorten debugging time and improve API behavior for callers.

lesson_sections.title: 4. Cleanup Paths: finally and Context Managers
lesson_sections.body: Some resources must be cleaned up even when errors happen. Use finally blocks or context managers (`with`) to ensure cleanup runs consistently. This prevents hidden leaks and inconsistent state.

lesson_sections.title: 5. Assertions and Test Structure
lesson_sections.body: Assertions encode expected behavior. A useful test suite includes normal cases, edge cases, invalid input, and boundary values. Prefer deterministic tests with clear failure messages over ad-hoc prints.

lesson_sections.title: 6. Debugging Workflow You Can Repeat
lesson_sections.body: A reliable debugging loop is: reproduce the bug, narrow input, inspect state, form a hypothesis, apply one change, rerun tests, and confirm outcome. This process scales better than random edits under pressure.
